pages.name: Two copies of the current
pages.text: The heat each second in a wire is `P = I²R`, where `I²` is the current used twice, one copy along each side of a heat tile. Double the current and both sides double. The heat fills a 2 by 2 square, four tiles, not two.

pages.name: Three times the current
pages.task: The same resistor carries three times the current. How many times the heat?
pages.why: Both copies of the current in `I²` are three times as big, so the heat is a 3 by 3 square: `3² = 3 × 3 = 9` tiles.

pages.name: Light spreads out
pages.text: A small lamp gives a quarter of the light at twice the distance, `2⁻² = ¼`: an [[inverse square law]] (OpenStax). One way to picture it: the same light spreads over a patch twice as wide and twice as tall, four squares, so each square gets a quarter.

pages.name: Three times as far
pages.task: Move the lamp three times as far away. What does each square get now?
pages.why: Three times as far, the patch is 3 wide and 3 tall, 9 squares. The same light shared over 9 squares gives each `3⁻² = ⅑`.

pages.text: Engineering notes (Purdue, WPI) give the gas law `pVⁿ = C`, where n is a fixed number and `n = 1` is Boyle's law. pages.name: An eighth of the power
pages.task: A pump with no height to lift must take only ⅛ of its power. What share of its speed should it run at?
pages.why: The power goes with the speed cubed, so run it backwards with a cube root: `∛⅛ = ½`, because `½ × ½ × ½ = ⅛`. A block half as wide, half as tall and half as deep holds ⅛ of the first.

pages.name: The lamp at half the distance
pages.task: A lamp is brought to half the distance. What does each square get now?
pages.why: At half the distance the patch is half as wide and half as tall, a quarter of a square. So each square gets `0.5⁻² = 4` times the light.
